caption: Matching with transmission lines, with the pool's worked numbers. Section 1: the quarter-wave transformer (Q-section) inverts its load, Z_in = Z0 squared over Z_load, so the section's impedance is the geometric mean of line and load - matching a 100-ohm feed point to a 50-ohm line wants sqrt(50 x 100) = 70.7 ohms, and the suitable line is 75 ohms (E9E06; the 62-ohm choice is the arithmetic-mean trap). Section 2: the half-wave line repeats its termination - the input sees the load unchanged, so a shorted far end shows up as very low impedance (E9F04); an air-insulated half-wave line at 14.10 MHz is 300/14.10 = 21.3 m over 2 = 10.6 m (E9F06). Section 3: a stub match is a short length of line connected in parallel with the feed line at or near the feed point (E9E03), and its behavior follows the same rules - lambda/8 shorted is inductive (E9F10), lambda/8 open is capacitive (E9F11), lambda/4 shorted is very high impedance (E9F09), lambda/4 open is very low (E9F12), lambda/2 shorted is very low (E9F04). Finding where the stub goes and how long to cut it is the Smith chart's classic job (E9G05).
spoken: Three panels. First, the quarter-wave transformer: a 50-ohm feed line runs into a heavier quarter-wave Q-section of 75-ohm line, then a 100-ohm load; the quarter wave inverts, so the section impedance is the square root of 50 times 100, about 70.7 ohms - use 75-ohm line. Second, the half-wave line: it repeats its termination, so the input sees the load unchanged; at 14.10 MHz a wavelength is 21.3 meters, so a half-wave air-insulated line is 10.6 meters. Third, a grid of stubs: shorted stubs are inductive at one-eighth wave, very high impedance at one-quarter, very low at one-half; open stubs are capacitive at one-eighth, very low at one-quarter, very high at one-half. A stub is just a short piece of line in parallel at the feed point, and the Smith chart tells you where to put it and how long to cut it.
